title: Americans are using AI as a practical life infrastructure while fearing losses of purpose, agency and human connection
source_unit: Imagining the Digital Future Center at Elon University, Human Purpose in Peril national public-opinion poll
geography: United States adults, including large language model users and demographic subgroups

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in nationally representative survey, including 1163 LLM users and an oversample of 501 LLM users

human_connection_concern.unit: per cent saying AI will weaken human-to-human bonds a lot or somewhat

purpose_concern.unit: per cent agreeing AI replacing humans in most tasks will undermine purpose and meaning, versus 36 per cent choosing the purpose-enhancing alternative

agency_confidence.value: 55 per cent are not confident people will retain critical-thinking and information-evaluation ability; 46 per cent are not confident people will maintain motivation and purpose.

institution_first_frame.value: The report argues that individual resilience is insufficient and that institutions must help people preserve agency during AI transition.

observations.method: National public-opinion survey conducted May 14-18, 2026, with an LLM-user oversample; overall margin of error reported as plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
observations.uncertainty: These are expectations and confidence judgments, not observed changes in social connection, cognition, purpose or institutional performance; the oversample makes LLM-user estimates analytically useful but requires attention to weighting and subgroup precision.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults and LLM users by age, race and ethnicity, gender, employment, education, parental status and party identification.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI may alter the form of social connection and meaning without reducing them; fears of dehumanization may coexist with new learning, creativity and communication capabilities.

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026 fieldwork; weekly LLM use and personal-agent adoption

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the national survey

weekly_llm_use.unit: per cent saying they used an LLM in the past week, up from 52 per cent in early 2025

personal_agent_adoption.unit: per cent of LLM users who have built a custom AI agent; 36 per cent among adults ages 18-29

everyday_influence.unit: per cent saying AI already heavily influences daily routine or will do so within five years

nonuse_boundary.unit: per cent expecting AI will never significantly affect them

observations.method: National survey of U.S. adults with questions about recent LLM use, custom agents and expected everyday influence.
observations.uncertainty: Weekly use does not establish intensity, quality, dependency, economic benefit or control over models; custom-agent construction may range from experimentation to sustained delegation.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by age, race and ethnicity, gender, work status and parental status; LLM users are analyzed separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid adoption can reflect low-cost experimentation and useful assistance rather than deep social displacement; reported nonuse may change as access and awareness spread.

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026 fieldwork; AI as personal advisor and decision infrastructure

denominator.unit: LLM users in the survey, with reported use of bots for personal and business needs

informal_learning.unit: per cent of LLM users using chatbots for self-directed informal learning

product_research.unit: per cent of LLM users using chatbots for product research

life_decision_use.value: LLMs played a role for users in managing a medical condition (49%), upgrading job skills (44%), navigating a career change (34%), major financial decisions (29%) and selecting a place to live (17%).

social_rehearsal.unit: per cent of LLM users using chatbots to roleplay or practice personal encounters

observations.method: Survey questions about LLM applications among respondents who used an LLM in the prior week.
observations.uncertainty: Reported assistance is not verified advice quality, clinical safety, financial suitability, housing outcome or durable behavior change; the cross-sectional design cannot show whether bots replace or supplement human institutions.
observations.subgroup: Recent LLM users, including people using bots for health, work, finance, housing, shopping, learning and interpersonal preparation.
observations.counterinterpretation: LLMs may extend access to information and rehearsal for people who lack time, money or trusted human guidance, even while introducing accuracy and overreliance risks.

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026 fieldwork; benefits, dependence and institutional guidance

denominator.unit: LLM users for user-experience measures; 1505 U.S. adults for institutional-confidence measures

benefit_learning.unit: per cent of LLM users saying they routinely learn something new and valuable from AI

shortcut_risk.unit: per cent of LLM users saying they felt lazy or took an easy shortcut at least some of the time

verification_behavior.unit: per cent of LLM users actively cross-checking AI accuracy against non-LLM sources

institutional_confidence.value: 39 per cent of all adults rate AI companies extremely or very effective in helping people adapt; comparable high-confidence shares are 34 per cent for higher education, 26 per cent for K-12 education and 27 per cent for employers, while confidence is lower for legal systems and governments.

observations.method: Survey of LLM-user experiences and U.S. adult expectations about institutions' ability to guide adaptation.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported benefits, harms and verification do not establish actual accuracy or dependency; institutional ratings measure expectations and may reflect prior trust, ideology or familiarity.
observations.subgroup: LLM users and U.S. adults evaluating technology firms, education, employers, law, government and religious institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Users may develop practical verification norms and institutions may build new forms of guidance; low confidence in governments does not necessarily mean low demand for public regulation.

related_sources.claim: Official report landing page, key findings and survey framing.
Official survey topline and methodology document.

boundary: This record adds a public meaning-and-agency layer to the broader AI trend stream: Americans are adopting LLMs for learning, shopping, health, work, finance, housing and social rehearsal while worrying about purpose, connection, critical thinking, dependence and institutional guidance. It is a nationally representative U.S. adult survey with an LLM-user oversample, not a longitudinal behavioral study, clinical or economic outcome evaluation, or proof that AI causes social fragmentation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ITDF Human Purpose in Peril report PDF was reviewed for sample design, LLM adoption, human-connection and purpose concerns, agency confidence, user benefits and harms, personal-agent use, life-decision use, verification behavior and institutional effectiveness expectations.
